segments.t: Good morning, Morgan. I am at NVIDIA's GTC conference here in Berlin, and I have none
other than Jensen Wong, the CEO of NVIDIA. Jensen, thank you so much for making the
time. You've had a busy morning. We're here in Europe. You've been traveling around
London, Paris, all of these different cities around Europe. You've announced around $10
billion worth of investments across the continent into around 14 startups. What are the thematics
behind those investments? What's getting you excited? Well, we're trying to create
kickstart the AI economy in Europe. Of course, you know, Europe has a tremendous
amount of technology, tremendous amount of industrial know-how, incredible science and
technology, and it's ready to engage and build the AI economy here. In order to build the AI
economy, you need to invest in all five layers of that industry. Energy, chips, infrastructure,
the models, and of course, all of the AI applications. Each one of the industries,
every single company here in Europe is going to become an AI company someday.
I'm thinking that in five years' time, whether you're a media market here in Germany,
Mercedes or Siemens or Merck, all of these companies are all going to HSBC. They're all
going to HSBC. They're all going to become AI companies, and so we're just accelerating that
journey, a journey that we started a couple of years ago, and it's really picking up.
Europe, like many other places in the world, has several challenges, whether it's access to
capital, whether it's energy prices. There's often this discussion around who is strong in
AI, the US or China, and there's this view that Europe kind of gets sidelined in that
discussion. Does Europe have what it takes, given some of those challenges, to compete with
what we're seeing out of China, what we're seeing out of the US in terms of AI
capability companies? Absolutely. The most important thing about leadership in AI is actually
the application of the technology in your industry, and so whoever has whatever region,
whatever country, defuses AI most and quickly will ultimately win. And the reason for that is
because you want to lift the entire industry, every single industry, with AI, not just create
a new industry of a few companies, and so you want every part of your economy to be accelerated by AI.
Tipton, the market always loves to hear what you have to say about the state of play of the
industry across the board, and at the moment, there feels to be a bit of nervousness in the
market, and particularly around neoclouds. We've seen end scale, looking at investors
selling it to reduce its valuation, farmers pulling its IPO, concerns over the debt levels
of some of these neoclouds. Is there a problem right now with the neocloud business model,
or are these just teething issues? If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neoclouds
is off the charts. Their capabilities are extraordinary, and so what is missing in
the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth, to fund that growth, and because there's
just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital. The demand of the
capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved,
and that's going to get solved because, fundamentally, the most important things
are the values that these guys are providing, these companies are providing,
the demand for it is so strong. Just given the number of plays in this paper,
there's dozens of companies described as neoclouds. Do you expect any kind of
consolidation and M&A to take place in this particular sector of the industry?
Ultimately, they need scale. They need regional excellence. For example, here in Europe,
the energy is scarce. It's scarce everywhere, but you want to allocate the energy to your own
companies, and in the case of the UK, they want to allocate their energy to Enscale. In the case
of France, they want to allocate their energy to Mistral. Around the rest of Europe, allocate
your energy to Nebius. There's a fundamental reason why you want to make sure that your natural
resources are dedicated, allocated to your own companies first. If the neoclouds in Europe
are able to establish an infrastructure here, then you can build the AI ecosystem,
the AI economy on top of them, and then the flywheel of the AI economy will start in Europe.
It will terminate in Europe. You can bring investments into Europe, but you have to start
with having your own infrastructure. Do you think that scale comes from some form of consolidation
to grow those big plays? Right now, you have so much demand. I think you have more than
several companies you could start up. Of course, each one of the countries probably don't need
more than a couple, but across all of Europe, you're going to need a lot more neoclouds.
The working capital part of the equation is an interesting one, Jensen, because obviously
earlier this year, you, along with a number of financial players, announced this sort of
$500 billion financing mechanism. What is the demand at the moment for that? Is that something
that can be tapped as these neoclouds look to scale? Well, that's ultimately what we need.
One of the things that we're trying to do is to establish NVIDIA's compute as a financeable
asset. The residual value of our compute, because it's fungible, it's so productive,
it's so fungible, and it's so durable, it is now becoming an asset class. The more that
the institutions recognize this, the more that the lenders recognize this, the more
the capital will become available to the neoclouds. And so we're working to establish
that NVIDIA compute is really a fungible, productive, durable, financeable asset,
and I think that's going to be a game-changer. Jensen, what's your take on the current health
of the Frontier Labs at this point? There was a lot made about Anthropic's Q3 numbers,
45% growth, a lot of people saying, well, this is a significant slowdown from what we've seen at
the same time. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are aiming for these very highly valued IPOs.
Just wanted to get your take on whether you're worried about any kind of slowdown at the Frontier
Labs and are they going to be able to justify those valuations in the end?
We're looking at two of the most consequential technology companies in history,
incredible management team, incredible technical skills, incredible technical capability.
They're also the two fastest growing technology or any company in human history.
And so we could nitpick around the corners. I don't think it's maybe interesting,
but it doesn't change the fundamentals. We're talking about AI, which is the most consequential
technology in history, two of the most consequential technology companies in history,
incredibly well-built, and also the fastest growing ever. And so I think that's all that
matters. I know you've been talking a lot about safety and around social and societal impact
of this technology. One of the most interesting discussions has been around how do AI companies
do good for society. And Anthropic came out and said, hey, we're going to commit 5% of our shares
to a new public benefit fund, something that Elon Musk backed and said, we're going to give kids
in America some SpaceX shares. Have you considered any kind of initiative like this at NVIDIA?
We do all kinds of things for social good, and everybody has their own way of doing it.
The most important thing, you talked about AI safety, the most important thing that we need
to do as an industry is to create an optimistic future, but do it responsibly. This technology
has the potential to do incredible good. Whatever industry you choose, whatever economy you choose,
whatever country you choose, there is an extraordinarily optimistic and exciting future,
but we have to build this technology responsibly. One of the most important things that we've done
is created this technology called OpenShell. Anthropic is a very early adopter of it,
very enthusiastic collaborator, really appreciate their collaboration. We all want to see this
technology advance in the safest possible way, and we have the technology and the responsibility
to do so. Yeah, I don't think I'm pretty sure I'm going to second, Jensen, but just in terms of this
kind of broader discussion about how to give back, do you think this sort of direct equity method
is a good path to go down? The best way for those companies to give back is to contribute
in the way that they fundamentally contribute. Elon's best way to give back is to inspire a
whole generation to build things, heavy industries, launching rockets to space. What could be
more consequential and inspirational than that way of giving back? Anthropic's way of giving back,
number one, is to advance this technology, invent this technology, and bring it to the world safely.
The way NVIDIA gives back is all of the things that we're doing here, supporting the global
economy, helping every industry thrive, new companies to be created, invest in inspirational
entrepreneurship. That's our way of giving back. The best way to give back is to help the economies
grow. The best way to give back is to create new economies. Jensen, your view on the safety issue
really is that if a company believes that a model is dangerous, they should just not release it,
right? There doesn't need to be some kind of new broad regulation, etc. How can the general public
trust the leaders of these companies to make that right decision? Because they're incentivized
to do so. Regulations take a while to come. If there are concerns that exist today, it is your
responsibility to take responsibility and do something about it now, instead of waiting for
laws and regulations to happen, which takes time, as you know. And so the reason why I trust them to
do so is, one, I believe in the leadership. Two, I believe that the companies are incentivized
to do the right things, because there's no such thing as a good product that's not safe. And so
it is absolutely perfectly aligned incentives for their company to advance the technology
as responsibly as necessary. And part of the solution you have is open shell, right? Is
being able to monitor these models. To contain the monitor. Yeah, because one of the issues
we've seen is these models doing things they're not supposed to. And so how do you control that?
To contain it and to monitor it. And just continuously, look, here's what it's doing.
Here's what it's accessing. It's exactly the same way you think about a baby in a play pen.
You contain the baby and you monitor it. Now, the technology, of course, is very sophisticated.
And there's active monitoring and active controls that are part of this containment system.
It's as if it's like a super smart force field around AI. And then you have multiple layers of
it. And so it's not as if one layer is the end of this end of the story. Open shell is the first
layer. And then there's century, the second layer. And then you're going to have multiple layers of
defense. And so open shell is really critical. And you're confident this is going to stop some
of the issues we've seen, such as these unintended hacks and access into websites, etc. We're
confident that it would have handled the incidents we've seen. And we don't know what we don't know
about the future, but the technology was built on great first principles. We also have the advantage
of over a hundred companies around the world, including anthropic and open AI and SpaceX
and meta and Google and Microsoft and IBM and Red Hat and, you know, CrowdStrike and
Polito Networks, the world's leading operating system companies, cyber security companies and
frontier lab companies are all part of this open shell initiative contributing to it. And so
we've got the best minds in the world working on this one concept, one issue, one initiative.
And I can't imagine a more powerful coalition of bright minds around the world who want the same
thing. We've got a few minutes left, so I just want to get your take also on another big topic,
which of course is China, a lot of focus on some of the innovation coming out of that market.
For NVIDIA specifically, do you believe now this market is effectively closed for your chips?
Well, no market is closed forever. And China wants foreign companies to invest in China,
just as Germany wants foreign countries, companies and countries to invest in Germany. And so the
market has to be open and has to be welcoming. There's no reason to believe that that market
is going to be closed to the best competitors in the world. And NVIDIA is surely the best
in the world doing what we do. And we have a lot to offer and we're going to go compete
in China and around the world. And so to the extent that that market could be open to us,
we'd really appreciate it. Otherwise, we're going to continue to be here and we'll keep looking
for opportunities. It's a really interesting stride in the semiconductor industry in China.
In all different facets, CXMT, the memory company, is reportedly developing HBM3E now.
Is there a world in which you could partner with CXMT, use their HBM3E and some of your
older products to regain access to the market in a bigger way? Is that something you consider?
Of course, we're open-minded. We work with Chinese companies. Just about the whole world
works with Chinese companies in the supply chain somewhere. And whether it's empowered generation
or cooling technology or solar technology or battery technology, China is incredible at the
fundamental infrastructure technology. And no country collectively is better at manufacturing
than China. And so we have to take their capabilities very seriously.
And just in terms of the strides the Chinese semiconductor industry has made,
how would you assess those given what we're seeing at a company like Huawei?
Well, we've definitely accelerated because of all the regulations. We've accelerated
their internal capabilities probably 10 years and made it five. And so we've definitely
accelerated China's initiatives. It's nationalization of, if you will, semiconductor
manufacturing capabilities and all of the industrial support that has been put into that
sector. And so there's no question we've accelerated that. But nonetheless,
Nvidia's and American technology companies are mighty in this area. We're ready for
competition from all over the place. And we can take on competition from anybody.
Just as you look at your supply chain, memory, of course, is one of the key bottlenecks as
there are lots of bottlenecks across the supply chain.
Well, one of the most challenging bottlenecks is substrates.
This week, we announced that we're expanding our substrate capacity as large as it already is
by two and a half times more in the next three years. And so we're expanding our substrate
capacity as one of our most challenging limiters today. We're going to increase that by two and
a half times. IBM, UMTC, Semco, great partners of ours. And we're also expanding our co-os
packaging technology. And our work there with Amcor is going to increase our capacity tremendously.
And so we've this week announced a pretty sizable expansion of our supply chain.
And just on that memory story as well, Gens, it was a columnist in South Green who said,
well, there could be an oversupply of memory in 2029. Are you seeing any signs of that?
I don't think so. You know, one of the things that's really great about memory
is that you could always use more of it. And of course, through architecture ideas,
NVIDIA owns the architecture of our systems. Through architecture ideas,
we could shift around the resources as necessary. But HBM memory will be used for years to come.
And LPDDR, we're the first company in the world to put LPDDR memory, what goes into your cell phones,
into the world's data centers. And it's enabled us to deliver performance that is twice as energy
efficient as anything in the world today. And so we're going to continue to use abundant amounts
of that as well. Thank you, Jensen. It's been a pleasure speaking to you. Thank you so much
for taking the time to speak to you. What a great event. What's going on in Germany.
And don't don't if I could just have a second more. This week, we announced the expansion of our
supply chain. We we announced DGX pod, which accelerates the build out of the AI, AI factories.
We also announced open shell. I appreciate you giving me the chance to talk about AI safety.
And then we announced all of our initiatives here, particularly in Germany around physical AI,
so robotics and cars and telecommunications. Thank you for all of your insights. Thanks
to speak to you about a crazy schedule here. That was Jensen Wong, the CEO of NVIDIA.
Alright, I hope you're all doing well today and staying calm in this market. Thursday was a mixed
day in the market, and it was an especially rough day for AI stocks due to multiple factors.
First, there's the macro situation as tensions appear to have risen in the Middle East that
along with the subsequent action we saw in stocks resulted in treasury yields moving lower
as investors fled to safety. And then there were multiple news items that were specific to
the AI ecosystem. Meta reported strong earnings Wednesday evening showing solid growth in
advertising revenue and promising prospects regarding the future of Muse. That said,
Meta announced a new class of non-voting stock that they plan to use to raise capital,
which ultimately means dilution for shareholders. And leadership also said they expect Muse's total
serving costs to rise. Tesla reduced its 2026 capex forecast from $25 billion down to $20
billion. And Lamb Research reported earnings with next quarter revenue guidance coming in
just slightly above the consensus expectation but short of some of the more bullish expectations.
Lamb's CFO specifically said that next quarter revenue guidance would have been higher without
near-term supply chain constraints. And so, because the demand is so strong, Lamb only
reported next quarter revenue guidance that was slightly better than the consensus expectation
but not good enough to satisfy some of the ultra bullish expectations. I think the market's
reaction is very much an overreaction missing the forest for the trees. But all of the stuff
that I just mentioned put pressure on AI stocks Thursday as market participants are very nervous
right now when it comes to cost of capital, memory maker's pricing power, the viability of
Neocloud's business models and so forth. We're also less than two weeks away from an important
election, which is leading to even more volatility in a market than would normally be the case.
There's also been a lot of talk over the past 48 hours about critical vulnerabilities
that triggered a global cybersecurity emergency that added to the anxiety surrounding AI stocks
on Thursday. As I've said previously, I expect cybersecurity to be a major use case for AI that
drives a significant amount of token demand moving forward. With cybersecurity, we're talking about
an agentic workload that runs constantly generating 24-7 inference demand. And I don't see that
demand decreasing over time. I actually see it increasing over time as threats become more
numerous and complex. Now let's cover some news. On Thursday, NVIDIA launched Minerva to bring
end-to-end observability for AI factories. Minerva is a new AI ops platform built to
help teams find problems earlier and keep AI factories productive. It brings together telemetry
from infrastructure and AI workloads, then applies purpose-built AI models to turn that data into
timely actionable insight. Minerva focuses on AI factory yield, which is a measure of the useful
work infrastructure produces through GPU hours, good put, cluster uptime, and token production.
NVIDIA gave shout out to Iran in the press release saying that Iran is among the NVIDIA
partners using Minerva to optimize its AI factories. Iran announced on Thursday that they
will report earnings on Thursday, November 5th, after market close. As I've said in previous
videos, I continue to be bullish on Iran and likely will be through the first half of calendar
2028, depending on what happens. I think for this specific earnings report, AI cloud revenue
is likely to be somewhere in the range of $160 to $185 million, which is better than
the previous quarters of $70.5 million in AI cloud revenue. That said, I'm not expecting
this specific earnings report to be enough to satisfy market participants and move the stock
notably higher. That's something to potentially look forward to in calendar 2027. The main thing
I'll be looking for from Iran on November 5th is an update on their build out. There have
been some rumors recently that Iran is having to re-cable Horizon 1 due to a design change
requested by Microsoft after Microsoft accepted delivery of Horizon 1 from Iran. If the rumors
are true, then Horizon 1 is likely still billing because Iran delivered the data center
to spec and Microsoft accepted it before they made the rumor change. I don't know if the rumors
are correct or not, but I'm sure it will be brought up on the earnings call. Horizons 2 through
4 are likely still on track to be delivered by year end and I want a clear update on that.
I also want an update on the additional 40,000 GPUs Iran is targeting to have operational by
year end. If Iran is able to deliver on their ARR target by year end, then the earnings report the
company releases in May 2027 may be the first report that could potentially grab market
participants' attention in a positive way. I also noticed Supermicro introduced the NVIDIA
VeriCPU rack, which contains 256 Veri CPUs and is 100% liquid cooled. CPUs are very important for
agentic AI at scale and NVIDIA's VeriCPU is a new CPU built from the ground up specifically
for agents. The VeriCPU and standalone CPU racks are a great example of NVIDIA's foresight as they
were preparing for agentic AI years in advance. We have an update on a Micron Taiwan labor union
situation. As I mentioned earlier this week, the larger of the two labor unions reached an
agreement with Micron and canceled the mediation that was scheduled for October 22nd and that
was a positive development. The other union said they would hold a one-day strike this Thursday,
October 22nd and it appears that only 11 employees went on strike Thursday. That's not
a problem for Micron at all. The union that reached an agreement with Micron represents about
11,000 workers. The other union that held a strike on Thursday represents about 2,400 workers
and 11 of those workers went on strike Thursday. It appears that the union that held a strike on
Thursday is scheduled to continue negotiations with Micron this Friday. We also got some details
reported by Reuters about Micron's bonus plan. According to Reuters, Micron said that it will
introduce quarterly company performance link payments for employees worldwide from fiscal
2027. This new program will supplement Micron's annual incentive program. Micron said its quarterly
bonus pool would be linked to financial performance calculated using profit after tax
minus projected capital spending for the next quarter with fiscal 2026 as the baseline. It
will pay half in cash after results with arrest and shares vesting after one year. The union
that held a strike Thursday said it planned to ask members to vote on Micron's latest proposal.
We will see what happens in the days ahead. I expect this situation will eventually be resolved.
In other news, SK Hynix has completed its share buyback about one month ahead of schedule.
Additional shareholder return plans are to be unveiled when SK Hynix reports earnings on
October 28. The news that SK Hynix finished its buyback early appears to have led to some
short-term selling in South Korea on fears that SK Hynix support is no longer present in the
market. I honestly think that's the wrong way to view things. Let's not miss the forest for
the trees. They completed the buyback early and they are expected to reveal additional shareholder
return plans next week. That is not a reason to panic at all. Now, in case you missed
Wednesday night's video, I actually posted it early Thursday morning because it took about 14
hours to make that video. Sorry about that. But in case you missed that video, let me recap some
of the highlights from Jensen Huang's GTC Berlin keynote so that we're all on the same page moving
forward. I'm just going to rapid fire important points that stood out to me from Jensen's keynote.
Jensen began by laying out the fact that NVIDIA is a full stack company innovating at every
single part of the stack through extreme co-design. Jensen mentioned that NVIDIA designed GPUs up until
Blackwell. Grace Blackwell was the first rack scale system and now with Vera Rubin NVIDIA
is taking it a step further. Vera Rubin processes beyond large language models to now processing the
entire agent. First, the agent has to think which is where the model comes in, perception,
reasoning, planning, and using tools. All of that runs on the large language model. Second,
the agent has what's called a harness, which is essentially the exoskeleton which orchestrates
the work. It allows the agent to engage memory and activate tools. Third is a computer design
for data processing that processes knowledge. And lastly, a computer dedicated to CUDAX libraries
and its job is to run tools. And these computers now represent the entire agentic system. Jensen
said Vera Rubin is in full production. It's the first computer NVIDIA has created with no cables,
no wires. It's completely liquid cooled and it processes the entire agent. Jensen said that it
used to take two hours to assemble one node in the case of Grace Blackwell with cables and wires
everywhere and it was 80% liquid cooled. And now Vera Rubin is 100% liquid cooled and it takes
less than five minutes to assemble. That is incredible. That translates to higher cycle times,
much better reliability and much better performance. Jensen announced NVIDIA DSxPods.
From investor's perspective, this is probably the most important announcement from the keynote,
in my opinion. I want you to pay close attention to this one because this is honestly a genius
move on NVIDIA's part. I think this will be a major success and it has massive implications
for the entire AI ecosystem. Seven liquid cooled Vera Rubin compute racks connected with 17
kilometers of spectrum X cables form a Vera Rubin DSxPods. Vera Rubin DSxPods are integrated,
fully cabled and factory tested. They're then delivered in transportable containers.
Dry coolers replace traditional evaporative cooling. 800 volts DC connect to the racks for
efficient power delivery. One site utilities are ready. Estimated on-site deployment goes
from several months down to just days. Now with DSxPods, AI factories can be built much faster
with much less time to first token. This is honestly genius. I think this is going to be a
major success for NVIDIA. Essentially, NVIDIA has created an option by which companies don't
have to build the physical shell of the data center. Almost everything comes pre-packaged,
integrated, fully cabled, factory tested and ready to go. The transportable container effectively
serves as the shell, replacing the massive buildings that normally have to be constructed
when an AI factory is built. This will likely be a very popular option among Neo clouds,
as well as hyperscalers. Jensen made the point that with Grace Blackwell,
NVIDIA took rack assembly that was previously done on-site at AI factories and NVIDIA moved
that assembly into the supply chain so that customers building AI factories wouldn't have to
do all of that assembly on-site. And now NVIDIA is taking it a step further by moving the assembly
of almost the entire data center into the supply chain. Everything will be fully assembled,
integrated, tested, burned in and shipped all in a single ready to go package and it will
substantially reduce the amount of cabling and assembly that has to be done on-site. Jensen said
this is going to substantially reduce the amount of idle compute in data centers. If you're
building a one gigawatt data center and that site is delayed by just three months, that's
about $10 billion worth of missed revenues. But now by moving all of that assembly and cabling
into the supply chain, the amount of idle compute is going to be drastically reduced. Think about
what's happening here. NVIDIA is essentially assembling and shipping entire ready to go AI
factories. I fully expect this to be a major success for NVIDIA and it has important
implication for the AI build out and the entire AI ecosystem. This is especially fantastic
for the Neo clouds that are relying heavily on debt to fund their build outs. With these Neo
clouds, there's greater execution risk and time to first token is extremely important given their
heavy reliance on debt. NVIDIA is removing a lot of that execution risk and speeding up the time
to first token. Jensen said that by moving all of this assembly into the supply chain, NVIDIA can
reduce a one gigawatt AI factories time between installation of compute to the generation of the
first tokens from four, five months down to just one month. That is fantastic. Again, for a one
gigawatt AI factory, that means companies will be able to capture about $10 billion of revenue
they otherwise would have missed out on due to the time gap between compute installation and the
generation of the first tokens. This is a really big deal and I'm very excited about what this
means for the entire AI ecosystem and all the companies involved. This will likely be an
important accelerant to the entire build out. Jensen said that because of DSxPODs, quote,
velocity goes up, the wasted idle compute, the wasted idle capex will reduce and everyone
becomes more profitable. I also think this will be great for companies like iron that have a very
large secure power portfolio as it will greatly speed up time to first token and could enable
them to monetize that power portfolio sooner than was previously expected. In a press release,
NVIDIA said they are working to deliver DSxPODs worldwide, starting in early 2027. Jensen also
spoke about the importance of open models and he said that in the future, every company will
use both closed models as well as open models that they customize. As I've said many times,
open models are great for NVIDIA's business and at the same time, there will continue to be
demand for leading frontier intelligence for the most demanding use cases. Jensen made the point
that NVIDIA's open models are not necessarily the frontier of frontiers. However, with customization
and the help of ecosystem partners, companies can turn NVIDIA's open models into frontier and turn
their own proprietary data into sovereign intelligence. Jensen shared multiple examples
of companies taking this approach and customizing NVIDIA's open models using
their own proprietary data so that the resulting models are comparable or even exceed frontier
capabilities. Jensen reiterated that the idea that AI will result in the end of software
companies is incorrect. It's exactly the opposite. He says there will be more users
of these tools than there have ever been before. Every single tools company will now become an AI
company, an agents company. Not only will they offer tools, but they will also offer specially
optimized agents that are incredibly good at using their tools. Jensen said just about every
enterprise is building agents and working with NVIDIA to do so. Jensen also spoke about
physical AI and self-driving vehicles, which is the first high-volume physical AI application.
He announced that four more lines are going to be compatible with NVIDIA's drive Hyperion
and be part of the ride-hailing network Robo Taxi Fleet. Many other details were shared
throughout the keynote. I would say from an investor's perspective, the most important
development is probably the announcement of Vera Rubin DSxPods and the implications
it has for the speed of the AI build out. It will likely be an important accelerant
to growth. Looking ahead, we have Alphabet and Microsoft earnings on October 28 and
then Amazon earnings on October 29. Let's briefly cover those companies as it relates
to NVIDIA and CapEx ahead of their earnings. Last quarter Alphabet said they expect 2026
CapEx to be in the range of $195 to $205 billion and they said, quote,
we continue to expect our CapEx to increase significantly in 2027. Google Cloud has been
showing very impressive growth with revenue up 82% last quarter. Alphabet has a strong
incentive to increase CapEx and the company has many valuable use cases for compute.
I expect Alphabet's CapEx guide to be strong given their previous comments,
GCP's impressive growth rate and the fact that Alphabet has so many different
use cases for the compute they bring online. Now let's talk about Microsoft.
So last quarter Microsoft said it expects calendar 2026 CapEx to be roughly $175 billion,
which was down from the previously announced $190 billion. The downward adjustment to the
CapEx guide was made because moving forward, more of Microsoft's future data center leases
will shift from finance leases to operating leases. Operating leases are included in OpEx,
not CapEx, which is why Microsoft reduced their CapEx guide, even though they still
expect to spend money. Microsoft also said on the last earnings call that they expected fiscal
Q1 CapEx. So CapEx in the quarter that they report results for on October 28 to be over
$50 billion, which is notably higher than the previous quarter's $41 billion. Microsoft also
told us last quarter that they expect fiscal 2027 CapEx to increase year over year given
the strong demand signals across the portfolio. And the big news last quarter was that Microsoft
said it expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. Now I do expect Microsoft's
CapEx guidance to be strong given the strength we saw from Azure last quarter,
leadership commentary on their earnings call, and the fact that Microsoft is really making a push
with their own AI products and services. You may remember just last month Microsoft announced
a major overhaul of Microsoft 365 co-pilot with home code and autopilot. And they also
announced usage based billing for more compute intensive AI features. So Microsoft needs more
capacity to fulfill its massive cloud backlog worth hundreds of billions of dollars. And they
also need a lot of capacity for their own models, products and services. I expect Microsoft's
CapEx commentary to be positive overall. And then there's Amazon. Last earnings season,
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy laid out a great case for how Amazon is monetizing new capacity as soon as
it comes online. They have clear line of sight to strong financial returns on their investments.
And there's far more demand than what they can supply. AWS is the largest cloud, by the way.
Last quarter, AWS hosted accelerating revenue growth and expanding operating margin,
